title: Nonblocking KV prefetch & throughput sweep: TRT-LLM vs vLLM on private cluster
next_steps: Samir to share detailed benchmark spreadsheet and runbook
Lina to provision TRT-LLM tuned container for HelmBank private cluster trial
Customer to provide NVLink-enabled node access for 10/12-10/19 perf runs
action_items: Lina Gomez: produce nonblocking CUDA-graph test harness and baseline scripts; due 2027-10-11

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05
Start: 15:00 PDT (US West)
Duration: ~67 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording available)
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Omar (Redwood SE), Markus (HelmBank ML Infra), Priya (HelmBank Platform), Ethan (HelmBank SRE), Sara (HelmBank Security)
Recording link: https://meet.redwood/recordings/ff-20271005-helmbank

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to align on a throughput/latency sweep using nonblocking CUDA graphs and KV prefetch patterns across TRT-LLM and vLLM on HelmBank private/NVLink-enabled nodes. Focus on kernel selection side-effects when combining quantization (4-bit) with aggressive batching, and how VPC/on-prem network constraints influence inter-node fallback. Decision goal: agree pilot scope, share benchmark harness, and get node access.

Topics:
- nonblocking CUDA graphs vs blocking replay
- KV cache prefetch strategies and async prefetch window sizing
- kernel path differences w/ TRT-LLM vs vLLM (FP16/INT8/4-bit quantized runs)
- batching tradeoffs for sub-50ms p99 vs throughput at 500-1000 rps
- private cluster profiling constraints (NVLink, NUMA, driver versions)
- security/compliance notes for on-prem trials

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: okay hi everyone thanks for carving out the time today, this is Samir from Redwood, with Lina and Omar on the call — hey folks?
[00:07] Markus: hey Samir, thanks. We've got Priya, Ethan and Sara on as well. we're excited to look at the nonblocking stuff, we've seen some noisy p99s when we try to scale.
[00:15] Priya: quick context — HelmBank runs a private cluster with mixed A100 and H100 nodes, NVLink within multi-GPU machines but not across racks. We want to see if we can get predictable latency for our chat assistant while keeping cost down.
[00:30] Lina: great, so today we'll walk through our proposed harness: a nonblocking CUDA-graph path that avoids host-device syncs during graph replay, plus a KV prefetcher that warms the cache async; and we compare TRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior under identical request mixes.
[00:45] Ethan: when you say nonblocking — do you mean we avoid cudaDeviceSynchronize in between launches? we suspect our existing pipeline does implicit syncs when we call malloc/free.
[00:53] Omar: yes, nonblocking here means we pre-record a set of graphs for common token lengths and then launch them with streams that use cudaGraphInstantiate/Launch without synchronizing at every token. the tricky bit is KV cache management across stream boundaries.
[01:12] Markus: uh-huh, okay. can you share what benchmarks look like? like single-stream p50/p99 vs multi-stream throughput?
[01:20] Lina: I'll paste the sample traces. Our baseline is vLLM with async batching at the operator level; TRT-LLM introduces different kernel selection — it tends to favor fused attention kernels on H100 when the sequence length is <512, but when we enable int8/4-bit quant it falls back to alternate kernels that change latency characteristics.
[01:39] Priya: are those fallbacks deterministic? we've seen variance that looks like kernel-switch jitter.
[01:45] Lina: partially deterministic — kernel selection depends on sequence length, quant mode, and heuristics for workspace size. on TRT-LLM the selection is at compile/inference time; vLLM's runtime scheduler does more dynamic dispatch which sometimes gives smoother tail latency but less throughput in tight-batch regimes.
[02:05] Samir: quick note — we've seen NVLink-enabled pinned KV cache gives big savings when you have multi-GPU context reuse. but in HelmBank's case, NVLink across racks is absent, so inter-node prefetch has to go over RDMA or TCP inside the VPC. that impacts fallback strategies.
[02:23] Sara: security question — if we enable RDMA-based KV prefetch, does Redwood require extra permissions or open ports? we need to ensure nothing breaks our SSO/SSM rules.
[02:31] Samir: we'll include a runbook with the required ports and a minimal privilege guide; for the pilot we recommend enabling prefetch inside the node (local NVLink) and using encrypted RDMA for cross-node if needed — we can provide KMS guidance.
[02:45] [00:03:00] Markus: can you walk us through typical numbers — like what do you see on H100 with nonblocking graphs at 4-bit quant and 8-token prompt?
[03:05] Lina: informal numbers: for a 7B-ish model at 4-bit with TRT-LLM on H100, we see p50 token latency ~6-8ms, p99 token latency jumps to 45-70ms under bursty arrival unless KV cache prefetch is warmed. vLLM for same model shows p50 ~8-10ms and p99 ~35-55ms — so vLLM trades a bit of p50 for more stable p99 in our tests, likely due to its dynamic operator fusion choices.
[03:36] Ethan: interesting — so TRT is faster in the median but can spike heavier — does that align with kernel change during sequence?
[03:44] Lina: exactly. for sequence lengths where TRT switches to a different attention kernel (say going beyond a tile size), you get a different workspace allocation pattern and potentially a device-side sync. nonblocking graphs reduce the host sync cost but they don't eliminate kernel-induced workspace growth which can cause eviction or cudaMalloc retries.
[04:05] Omar: and when quantized to 4-bit with per-channel scaling, some kernels become memory-bandwidth bound and then you see p99 blow up when eviction thrash happens in the allocator.
[04:18] [00:05:00] Markus: so for our pilot what should we try first — smaller batch sizes and longer warm-up? or aggressive batching?
[04:27] Samir: recommended sweep: 1) baseline single-stream nonblocking graph per-seq-len; 2) incremental concurrent streams (2,4,8) with KV prefetch window sizes (0ms, 50ms, 200ms); 3) batching policies: immediate dispatch vs wait-for-n tokens vs time-window; 4) quant modes: FP16, INT8 (if supported), 4-bit. That will expose where kernel switches cause tail spikes.
[04:51] Priya: for the KV prefetch window, do you have heuristics? 200ms seems large.
[04:57] Lina: heuristic: prefetch window equals expected inter-token time * token_count_in_next_turn + jitter buffer. For chat where user typing introduces delay, window can be 100-300ms. For pure server-side streaming we do 0-50ms. But larger windows can cause memory bloat.
[05:15] [00:07:00] Ethan: we've observed that our allocator backend is the default cuMemAlloc with fragmentation under sustained load — does Redwood recommend a different allocator?
[05:24] Omar: yes, we often recommend using a pooled device allocator (jemalloc-like) or CUDA's memory pool API with set memory affinity to avoid repeated cudaMalloc overhead. For TRT-LLM we've seen improvements with the CUDA memory pool when preallocating the worst-case workspace.
[05:42] Samir: note that using a pooled allocator can change the eviction behavior and hide kernel-worst-case; we document the tradeoffs in the runbook.
[05:50] [00:09:00] Markus: what about CUDA graphs stability — are there cases where replay fails because of dynamic-size tensors?
[06:00] Lina: dynamic shapes are the pain point. our nonblocking approach uses a small number of representative graphs (e.g., 8, 32, 128 token lengths) and chooses nearest graph. if you have shapes outside, we fall back to direct launches, which can spike latency. TRT-LLM had more rigid graph requirements in our tests, vLLM tolerated more dynamic operators but at some perf cost.
[06:21] Priya: can we instrument NVTX traces easily?
[06:25] Omar: yes, we'll give you an NVTX-enabled harness; it's critical to correlate cudaGraphLaunch latency to kernel selection. we recommend capturing per-kernel timing and the workspace sizes.
[06:35] [00:11:00] Sara: on compliance — we need audit logs for inference inputs/outputs retention policy. does Redwood's private deployment keep logs locally?
[06:44] Samir: for Private we leave log storage configurable; for the pilot we suggest turning on minimal tracing and storing it in your S3-compatible bucket inside the VPC with lifecycle policies. we'll share SOC2 docs separately.
[06:55] [00:12:00] Markus: were there any gotchas with NUMA on multi-socket nodes? we run dual-socket hosts for some clusters.
[07:02] Lina: yes: if CUDA is bound to CPU cores on the wrong NUMA domain you can get huge PCIe latency to the GPU. our probe scripts include numa-bind checks and will report cross-domain memcpy latency. for best results pin the host threads that drive the streams to the GPU-local NUMA nodes.
[07:22] Ethan: good to know. we've had subtle perf loss that was traced back to numa misbinding.
[07:27] [00:14:00] Priya: on the model side, do you recommend an explicit compile step for TRT-LLM? or live JITing from a container?
[07:35] Lina: TRT-LLM benefits from an AOT compile step per model variant because it lets TensorRT bake in the most efficient kernels for the target device. that said, containerized JITing helps for rapid iteration but risks different kernel choices on different driver versions. for the pilot we recommend AOT with pinned driver/kernel combination.
[07:53] Omar: and capture the engine with all the quantization options you plan to test — otherwise you'll see different engine selection which complicates comparisons.
[08:02] [00:16:00] Markus: can you give an example of a kernel mismatch that caused a big p99 delta?
[08:09] Lina: sure — on one H100 run the fused attention kernel used for 32-token sequences allocates a scratch buffer of 1.2GB when int8 is enabled. if multiple streams concurrently hit that path without prepopulated pools, you get per-stream allocation stalls. vLLM's operator split avoided that big single-scratch allocation and instead streamed smaller kernels which used bandwidth differently, resulting in lower p99 under the same concurrency.
[08:37] Sara: wow that is a big allocation, is that documented in TRT?
[08:41] Lina: not always; sometimes the workspace size comes from the kernel heuristics that are runtime-determined. we capture workspace sizes during profiling to identify those hotspots.
[08:50] [00:18:00] Ethan: about quantization — you said 4-bit earlier. how mature is 4-bit on TRT-LLM vs vLLM?
[08:58] Omar: vLLM has more conservative quant paths but they've invested in per-channel calibration which yields better numeric stability for 4-bit; TRT-LLM's int4 paths exist but are more experimental and sometimes fallback to slower kernels if the quantization layout isn't optimal. that can cause heterogenous kernel selection mid-batch.
[09:18] [00:20:00] Priya: so pilot plan would be to run the same prompt mix across all quant modes and measure token p50/p95/p99 and throughput at 1, 5, 10 concurrent streams?
[09:27] Samir: yes, and also measure memory high-water marks and number of cudaMalloc failures/retries. we usually log the allocator footprint and eviction counts.
[09:35] Markus: any recommended driver versions? or is that variable?
[09:39] Lina: we have a tested matrix: CUDA 12.4 + drivers X.Y for H100; but we will send the precise matrix. TRT engine compatibility is sensitive to minor driver changes, so pinning matters.
[09:52] [00:22:00] Priya: on the networking side — if we have to spill KV across nodes, what's the recommended protocol? RDMA or TCP?
[10:00] Omar: RDMA (GPUDirect) is better for latency but requires kernel/drivers and firewall rules. for initial pilot we recommend TCP within VPC with TLS, then profile RDMA as an optimization if cross-node latency is the bottleneck.
[10:14] Ethan: will RDMA require changes to the RL or KVS client?
[10:18] Lina: minimal changes — mostly transport configuration. but if you go GPUDirect RDMA you sometimes need a different allocator/adapter to do zero-copy transfers. we can provide an adapter.
[10:30] [00:24:00] Markus: curious about how Redwood detects kernel-induced jitter — do you have heuristics or automated alerts?
[10:37] Samir: Redwood Console's traces tag kernel families and will fire alerts when p99 deviation doesn't correlate with throughput; we also flag sudden workspace size increases in the timeline which often indicate a kernel change.
[10:49] Lina: we also run differential traces between TRT-LLM and vLLM to show where operator timings diverge. that helps debug whether it's a kernel selection issue or an allocator/NUMA issue.
[10:59] [00:26:00] Priya: what's the rough time for Redwood to stand up a TRT-LLM tuned container for our private cluster?
[11:05] Omar: if you grant us node access, we can produce a tuned container and a first-pass engine within 3-5 business days; the full sweep will take ~1-2 weeks depending on concurrency permutations.
[11:18] Priya: good. Markus, are we comfortable providing a test node?
[11:21] Markus: yes we can carve out a single NVLink H100 node for 10/12 onward. I'll follow up with Ethan.
[11:27] [00:28:00] Sara: security again — you mentioned runbooks and SOC2 docs; do you support on-prem KMS integration?
[11:34] Samir: yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and can configure the agent to use your internal KMS endpoints. we'll include the integration steps in the runbook.
[11:44] [00:30:00] Ethan: what's the fallback plan if cudaGraph replay causes nondeterministic failures under high concurrency?
[11:51] Lina: we have a fallback lane: if a graph launch returns an error we fall back to the direct-launch implementation and capture the trace. we also maintain a lightweight watchdog that throttles new stream launches until the allocator stabilizes.
[12:05] Markus: how do you surface those events in Console?
[12:09] Samir: Console will log the error, tag the request with fallback reason, and include the NVTX timeline. we'll show an example in the shared spreadsheet.
[12:18] [00:32:00] Priya: anything else we should be cautious of for multi-tenant nodes? we do co-location of other HPC workloads.
[12:25] Omar: co-located work can cause memory pressure and scheduler preemption; we recommend isolated GPU partitions or dedicated nodes for the pilot. if co-location is unavoidable, increase the prefetch window conservatively and run the jitter sweep at low concurrency first.
[12:43] [00:34:00] Samir: quick recap — action items: Lina builds nonblocking CUDA graph harness and NVTX-enabled traces; Samir sends SOC2 and pricing sketch; Markus/Ethan provide node access and sysinfo. run dates tentatively start 2027-10-12.
[12:59] Priya: that works. please include the exact driver/kernel matrix in the runbook.
[13:05] Lina: will do — I'll include a checklist: cuda, driver, GCC, NUMA pinning, RDMA prerequisites, and allocator flags.
[13:14] [00:36:00] Markus: one last question — is there a recommended tokenization alignment process so that both TRT-LLM and vLLM use identical token boundaries? we've seen off-by-one tokenization differences change kernel paths.
[13:23] Omar: yes, canonical tokenization config is critical. we recommend shipping a tokenization fixture file with the harness and verifying byte-level equality of token ids. we'll provide a sample harness to assert parity.
[13:36] [00:38:00] Priya: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[13:40] Samir: thanks all. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and the harness.
[13:45] [00:40:00] (meeting recording ends and short post-call audio)
